17.1: Arjuna asks: what of those who sacrifice with faith but disregard scripture — is their state sattva, rajas or tamas?
17.2: Faith is of three kinds, born of one's own nature — sattvic, rajasic and tamasic; hear of them.
17.3: The faith of each accords with their nature; a person is made of their faith — as the faith, so the person.
17.4: The sattvic worship the gods, the rajasic the demigods and demons, the tamasic ghosts and spirits.
17.5: Those who practise severe austerities not enjoined by scripture, driven by hypocrisy and egoism, full of desire, attachment and force —
17.6: — torturing the elements in the body and Me who dwell within — know their resolve to be demonic.
17.7: Food too is of three kinds, as are sacrifice, austerity and charity; hear the distinction.
17.8: Sattvic food increases life, purity, strength, health, joy and cheerfulness — savoury, oily, substantial and agreeable.
17.9: Rajasic food is bitter, sour, salty, very hot, pungent, dry and burning, causing pain, grief and disease.
17.10: Tamasic food is stale, tasteless, putrid, left over and unclean.
17.11: Sattvic sacrifice is offered according to scripture by those who desire no fruit, with the mind fixed on the duty itself.
17.12: Rajasic sacrifice is offered with an eye to fruit and for the sake of display.
17.13: Tamasic sacrifice is without scriptural sanction, without food offered, without mantra, without gift and without faith.
17.14: Austerity of the body: worship of the gods, the twice-born, teachers and the wise; purity, uprightness, continence and non-injury.
17.15: Austerity of speech: words that cause no distress, that are truthful, pleasant and beneficial, and regular study of scripture.
17.16: Austerity of mind: serenity, gentleness, silence, self-control and purity of nature.
17.17: This threefold austerity practised with supreme faith and without desire for fruit is called sattvic.
17.18: Austerity done for the sake of respect, honour and reverence, or with ostentation, is rajasic — unstable and impermanent.
17.19: Austerity done under a deluded notion, with self-torture, or to harm another, is declared tamasic.
17.20: Charity given as a duty to a worthy person who does nothing in return, at the right place and time, is sattvic.
17.21: Charity given reluctantly, or with a view to return, or looking for a reward, is rajasic.
17.22: Charity given at the wrong place and time to unworthy persons, without respect or with insult, is tamasic.
17.23: Om Tat Sat — the threefold designation of Brahman, by which the Vedas, the priests and the sacrifices were ordained of old.
17.24: Therefore acts of sacrifice, charity and austerity by knowers of Brahman always begin with Om.
17.25: With Tat, and without aiming at the fruit, the various acts of sacrifice, austerity and charity are performed by seekers of liberation.
17.26: Sat is used in the sense of reality and goodness, and also for a praiseworthy act.
17.27: Steadfastness in sacrifice, austerity and charity is also called Sat, and any action for their sake.
17.28: Whatever is offered, given or performed without faith is called Asat — of no account here or hereafter.
